claim: ADR-003 §6.3 names the case no shipped tier catches and rules that the change comes back unread. This file is that case, priced: the human still calls the after-image the same work, so the missed relink is real, and `catch: none` says the annotation can point at no mechanism in §6.2 that could have caught it. Every rate in the spike's `missed` column that is not a bug is one of these.

expect.note: §6.3 exactly: a rebase that edits the message *and* the file list. Strong, fallback and shape digests all move, no member commit survives, so nothing in §6.2 has a key to match on and the honest answer the ADR gives is `unread`.

events.note: One instance per annotated turn, because §6.3 is a clause about a shape and not about a favourite example. This family is the floor under the missed-relink column and the entire demand side of the case for a fuzzy tier.

expect.note: §5.3 and §2.6: authorship is one of the three facts, so all three digests move and the review state is lost by design. Scored as a miss because the work is the same work; the ADR accepts the price and `e4.1`'s aliasing is the remedy, so the spike's job is to say how large it is and not to relitigate §2.6.

events.note: A human amending an agent's commit and resetting the author in the same breath — `git commit --amend` after a cherry-pick onto a personal branch, which is what people actually do. The replacement identity is one nobody in the corpus already uses, so the rewrite really does move all three digests: an alias that already existed would be a different family (`e4.1`'s, and §2.6's namespace bump). Every turn in the corpus, because §2.6 makes it a rule and not a coincidence.

expect.note: ADR-003 §5.7 says a squash-merge whose subject was retyped rides on tier 3, a shared member commit. The annotation says: a squash mints one new commit and the two originals are not members of the surviving episode, so there is no shared member and tier 3 has no key either. Recorded as a carry owed and `catch: none`, which is the ADR's claim put to the test rather than repeated.
and even if a tier fired, RL0 and RL2 give the one landing to the first claimant; this verdict is stranded either way.

events.note: §5.7's PR squash-merge with a human-retyped title — the host pre-fills the title from the PR and the PR title is not either commit's subject, which is the case §5.7 nominates for tier 3.

expect.note: ADR-003 §5.6 files a squash under a brand-new subject with tier 3, "a shared member commit". A squash mints one new commit and neither original oid survives into it, so tier 3 has no key: the carry the ADR promises is not available, and the annotation says so rather than agreeing.

`address review: second round` is the verdict a reviewer would most expect to survive the squash — it is the sign-off that says the review round happened. It has one landing, no tier reaches it, and RL2 would have given that landing to t06 anyway.

events.note: A squashed PR merge on the authored stratum: t01 opened the parser, t03 addressed review on it, both over `src/flags.rs`, and the merge title is a third string again. Tier 2 cannot fire either: the merged episode's first member is a new commit whose path set is the union of both turns'.

expect.note: §5.10 predicts the member-set tier carries a split's surviving half because it shares a member with the original. The split mints two new oids, so nothing is shared — but the first half keeps the original's subject and author, so tier 1 gets there first and the carry is reachable after all. The annotation was wrong in the safe direction and says so now; what is actually lost here is the second half, below.

events.note: `git reset HEAD~1` and re-commit the change as two commits: one act, two new oids, and the original gone. `arrive_unread` is the corpus's only statement about a *live* episode: nobody ever reviewed `t02#2`, so a relink landing there is a false relink and its staying unread is the fail-visible answer §6.3 promises. Measured, the shipped pass does land on it — by `shape`, one event, one false relink, and the only §5.10 prediction this corpus contradicts.
